I wanted a way of getting a large number of recipes. A simple, one-and-done solution to the problem of "I don't know how to make X." Something like a wiki that provides database dumps, or some other large collection of formatted recipe data.

Then I thought of a way: the way I just said! The 'recipes' wikia offers database dumps: http://recipes.wikia.com/wiki/Special:Statistics

On that page, the line marked "current pages" links to a .7z which expands to 113 MB of XML consisting mainly of wiki markup, for which you would need a parser. And that's basically what you want, modulo the lack of explicitness of the data.

This, for example, doesn't distinguish between quantities and ingredients. The idea of an 'ingredient' is reified only by the wiki header markup. Sort of an *accidental* database that you can piece together while parsing the markup.

== Ingredients == * 1 cup cooked fava beans or canned fava beans * ½ cup [[lemon]] juice * 3 cloves [[garlic]] crushed with 1 tspn [[salt]] (optional) * 2 tbls finely chopped fresh [[Parsley]] * ½ cup olive [[oil]] I'm still curious if there's more out there that my searches didn't turn up. [kailo.biz](http://kailo.biz/opensourcecookbook/index.html), for example, is unsuitable:

>To download any recipe, simply click on the recipe name.

To download *all* the recipes, you'll have to get your hands dirty, and possibly get IP-banned from the site. So you're kinda stuck depending on this domain not to get struck by a comet, or co-opted by vegans who systematically delete all the recipes that include meat. Hence the preference for complete dumps.

I'd love to believe that the free market was capable of regulating itself against behavior like collusion, price fixing, and so on - but I think when you objectively look at the evidence there insufficient reason to believe such. Since the onset of capitalism we've had monopolies and other coercive behavior that invariably come at society's expense. Or today we can look to other countries. There are plenty of countries with impotent governments and the markets invariably end up monopolized once they 'evolve'. In places where the government is particularly small or ineffective the monopolization often extends beyond economic and 'metaeconomic' means and begins to include things such as threats of physical violence against those that would compete against it or their property.

Consequently, I think the thing that's going to go against the current trend of Voat politics is that some degree of market regulation is absolutely essential. And obviously this sort of regulation itself entails the possibility of regulatory capture, but I think that is less of a concern than the market without such efforts. For instance in the US Comcast obviously have succeeded in regulatory capture. The head of the FCC was a telecoms lobbyist and the president somehow thought it was a good idea to get multiple photo-ops of him parading around with Comcast's CEO, who also raised millions of dollars for him.

Nonetheless, Google has actually been able to compete even in that market. Their failures have been related to competing against an economic monopoly more than regulatory issues. They spend billions of dollars and months to years getting setup, and proudly announce they're going to offer comparable to better service for less. People pledge to swap over by the millions. The day before they launch Comcast/Time Warner/etc price and service match them. Nobody swaps over. Do you know how many customers Google Fiber has? Up to 120,000. They knew this would happen and are competing not for profit, but because their other businesses have an interest in improving the overall quality of telecoms access throughout the US. But the point there is that I think this is evidence that even regulatory capture is no where near as big a problem as straight forward economic means. The problem with regulatory capture is not what it does to competition, but the fact that it stops the government from enforcing price fixing, collusion, and other regulatory laws against the company in question. In essence with companies like Comcast we're getting a taste of the market as if there were no regulations at all in place, and I'm not too fond of that flavor.
